prime.problem: Each token's vector only describes that token. Before it can use the words around it, it needs a number for every other token saying how relevant that token is. And in training, a token that can see the next word will just copy its answer.
prime.fits: Builds on the dot product from One operation does almost all the work and on softmax from card 7. This card makes the scores; the next card turns them into weights with softmax and mixes the values.
expect: the causal mask (\(-\infty\) above the diagonal)
prime.goal: Compute any score of the tiny model by hand, explain with a measured number why scores are divided by \(\sqrt{d}\), and say exactly which cells are masked and why.

attend: Why does the model make a separate query and key from the same row of \(a\), instead of dotting the rows of \(a\) with each other?
Where does the \(3 \times 3\) shape of \(S\) come from, and what does one row of it mean?
As \(d\) grows, what happens to the spread of \(q \cdot k\), and what does that do to softmax's slope?
In training, which token would each position be cheating with if the mask were missing?
Why must the masked value be \(-\infty\) rather than 0 for the weights to come out right?

must: row of \(a\) times \(\Wq\) → query (what I'm looking for); times \(\Wk\) → key (what I offer) → score = query · key → big when the two point the same way → \(QK^\top\) gives every pair at once, \((3 \times 4)(4 \times 3) = 3 \times 3\)

\(q \cdot k\) sums \(d\) products → its spread grows like \(\sqrt{d}\) (2.007, 8.005, 29.898 at \(d = 4, 64, 896\)) → softmax of wide scores puts almost all weight on one key (0.868 vs 0.324 scaled) → slope \(A(1-A)\) near 0 (at most 0.0458) → gradients to \(\Wq\) and \(\Wk\) vanish → dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\) keeps the spread near 1

one pass predicts every next token at once → position \(t\)'s target is the input at \(t + 1\) → without the mask \(t\) could read its own answer → set later cells to \(-\infty\) → softmax gives them exactly 0 → training matches generation, where the future doesn't exist yet
elevated: The mask is \(-\infty\), not 0: softmax exponentiates, \(e^0 = 1\) would still give the future a share, while \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) removes it and the row still sums to 1
reference: np.triu(ones, k=1) marks the cells above the diagonal; PyTorch uses masked_fill
GPT-2 and Qwen2.5 both use head size 64, so they divide by 8
Qwen's \(\Wk\) is \(896 \times 128\) (2 shared key heads), its \(\Wq\) is \(896 \times 896\) (14 heads)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the \(3 \times 3\) score grid for the cat sat: label rows and columns, mark which cells are masked, and write next to it the equation that fills it and why it is divided by \(\sqrt{d}\). Or explain it in 4 sentences.
checklist: \(Q\) and \(K\) come from the same input \(a\) through two different learned matrices
each score is one query dotted with one key; \(QK^\top\) computes all of them
rows are the asking token, columns the token being scored
\(\div \sqrt{d}\) keeps the score spread near 1 so softmax doesn't saturate and gradients survive
cells above the diagonal are \(-\infty\) so no position sees a later token, its own target

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words what a query and a key are, and why a score is their dot product.
answer: query: what this token is looking for; key: what a token offers
both are learned projections of the same input row
a dot product is large when the two vectors point the same way, so a high score means a good match

retrieve.q: Walk through how \(S_{\text{raw}}[2,1] = 4.0013\) is made, starting from row 2 and row 1 of \(a\).
answer: row 2 of \(a\) times \(\Wq\) gives \(Q[2]\); row 1 of \(a\) times \(\Wk\) gives \(K[1]\)
row 2 is not masked at column 1, because cat comes before sat

retrieve.q: A colleague drops the \(\div \sqrt{d}\) because the model 'learns the right scale anyway'. What do you expect at \(d = 64\), and what does it cost?
answer: the \(q \cdot k\) spread is about 8 instead of 1
softmax becomes nearly one-hot: top weight about 0.868 vs 0.324
the slope \(A(1-A)\) is tiny, so \(\Wq\) and \(\Wk\) get almost no gradient early in training
the weights could shrink to compensate, but only if they get gradient to do it

retrieve.q: Why is the mask needed in training but not when generating one new token with a key cache?
answer: training scores every position in one pass, so later tokens are present and must be hidden
when generating, the new token's single query only meets keys that already exist
there is no future in the cache to hide

compare.q: Temperature divides logits by \(T\); attention divides scores by \(\sqrt{d}\). What do the two divisions have in common, what sets each value, and what goes wrong when each is too small?
answer: both shrink the inputs to softmax and so flatten its output
\(T\) is a choice at sampling time; \(\sqrt{d}\) is fixed by the head size to undo the growth of \(q \cdot k\)
too small a divisor (\(T = 0.5\), or no \(\div \sqrt{d}\)) makes the output nearly one-hot
for sampling that just means less variety; for attention it also kills the gradients

compare.q: Karpathy builds the mask from a lower-triangular matrix of ones; tiny.py marks the upper triangle with np.triu(k=1). Are these the same mask, and what would break if you used k=0?
answer: yes: keep on and below the diagonal, hide above it
k=0 would also hide the diagonal, so a token could not attend to itself
row 0 would then be all \(-\infty\), and softmax of all \(-\infty\) is nan

predict.q: Double every number in \(\Wq\) and leave the \(\div 2\) alone. What happens to row 2 of \(A\) (now \([0.1737,\ 0.8132,\ 0.0131]\))? Commit to a direction and a rough value.
predict.answer: Every query doubles, so every score doubles, which exactly cancels the \(\div 2\). Row 2 becomes \([0.0436,\ 0.9561,\ 0.0002]\), the same as deleting the scale. That is why the \(\sqrt{d}\) rule is about the spread of the scores at the start, not a fixed property: a model can learn its way back into the saturated region by growing \(\Wq\) and \(\Wk\).

apply.task: Fill in the rest of row 2 of \(S\) by hand. \(Q[2] = [-1.7157,\ -1.8983,\ 1.5939,\ -1.3733]\). \(K[0] = [0.1129,\ -0.8659,\ 0.5396,\ 1.0165]\) and \(K[2] = [-0.5212,\ 0.8141,\ -1.3733,\ 1.0271]\). Compute \(S_{\text{raw}}[2,0]\) and \(S_{\text{raw}}[2,2]\), divide by 2, then say which token sat attends to least and why it is still not masked.
apply.done: You get \(S_{\text{raw}}[2,0] = 0.9141\) and \(S_{\text{raw}}[2,2] = -4.2507\), scaled 0.4570 and −2.1253, matching tiny.out. sat scores itself lowest, and it is kept because a token may always see itself (\(j = i\)).
